deep.reconstruction:
Context. The heading reads m·f(r − αt)/r. This is the outgoing spherical-wave solution of the 3-D wave equation with propagation speed α, for a source of strength m. The same notation (α for the propagation speed, potentials of the form ∫ρ(t − r/α)/r) appears in Riemann's 'Ein Beitrag zur Elektrodynamik' (1858, printed 1867). The page is scratch work toward the potential of a moving point source at retarded time, i.e. the time t − r/α. It has no visible connection to the previous page on period moduli.

(1) Retarded position. Riemann writes √((x − (r/α)·∂x/∂t)² + …), the last factor struck out. This is the distance to the source's retarded position. To first order, x(t − r/α) ≈ x(t) − (r/α)·ẋ(t), and likewise for y and z.

(2) First-order displacement of 1/r. Moving one endpoint by (δx, δy, δz) gives
1/r + ∂(1/r)/∂x·δx + ∂(1/r)/∂y·δy + ∂(1/r)/∂z·δz = 1/r − (1/r²)(cos α·δx + cos β·δy + cos γ·δz).
Here cos α, cos β, cos γ are the direction cosines of r, using ∂(1/r)/∂x = −(x−x')/r³ = −cos α/r². With δx = −(r/α)ẋ, this is the retarded correction to the Coulomb term. A struck-out factor ·r/α shows that this substitution was intended.

(3) Temporal Taylor expansion. Viewing 1/r as a function of t and evaluating it at t − r/α gives
1/r − ∂(1/r)/∂t·(r/α) + ∂²(1/r)/∂t²·(r²/α²).
The first-order term is −(−ṙ/r²)(r/α) = ṙ/(rα); the marginal '+∂r/rr' records this. Since ∂(1/r)/∂t = −ṙ/r², the struck '−(∂r/∂t)/rr' is that derivative.

(4) Second derivative. Riemann writes
∂²(1/r)/∂t² = 2ṙ²/r³ − r̈/r²,
so the second-order term becomes (2ṙ²/r³ − r̈/r²)·r²/α² = (2ṙ² − r r̈)/(r α²).

(5) The last line, −4·ṙ·ṙ'/(rr) − [struck ∂²r/∂t²], appears to start collecting cross terms. These would come from combining the spatial (retarded-position) and temporal expansions, or from differentiating the product again. The line is fragmentary and its target cannot be determined with certainty.

Purpose (my inference). Expanding the retarded potential of a moving charge in powers of 1/α should produce velocity- and acceleration-dependent terms in ṙ²/α² and r r̈/α². This is the route by which Riemann (1858) and later Lorenz and Clausius recovered Weber-type laws, and it is the second-order (Darwin-type) expansion of the Liénard–Wiechert potential.
errors: The second-order Taylor term is written ∂²(1/r)/∂t²·r²/α² without the factor 1/2. A naive expansion of g(t − τ) has +τ²/2·g''. The omission may be a slip or a deliberate placeholder; the implicit dependence of τ = r/α on t could also alter coefficients.
Notational clash: α denotes the propagation speed and also the direction angle (cos α). It is harmless here but confusing.
Sign conventions for δx and for ∂(1/r)/∂x depend on which endpoint is moved; the page does not fix this.
The final line (−4 ṙṙ'/rr …) is fragmentary and its coefficient 4 cannot be verified from what is written.

results.what: Spherical wave m f(r − αt)/r as solution of the wave equation with speed α
results.modern_name: d'Alembert spherical wave / retarded potential kernel
results.usually_credited_to: Euler, d'Alembert, Poisson (18th–early 19th c.); retarded potentials in electrodynamics: Riemann 1858, L. Lorenz 1867

results.what: Expansion of 1/r at retarded time t − r/α in powers of 1/α, including ∂²(1/r)/∂t² = 2ṙ²/r³ − r̈/r²
results.modern_name: Post-Coulomb (Darwin-type) expansion of the retarded/Liénard–Wiechert potential

results.what: First-order change of 1/r under displacement: −(1/r²)(cos α δx + cos β δy + cos γ δz)
results.modern_name: Gradient of the Newtonian potential / directional derivative

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine scratch computations consistent with Riemann's known 1858 retarded-potential derivation of Weber's law. The only possible interest is if this sheet dates it earlier, but the page itself proves nothing new.

∂(1/r)/∂x = −cos α / r² with cos α = x/r (gives 0)
Taylor expansion g(t−τ) = g − τg' + τ²/2 g'' + …; exposes the missing factor 1/2 on the page

transcription_corrections: Marginal '+∂r/rr' is most likely '+ (∂r/∂t)/(rr)', i.e. the value of −∂(1/r)/∂t; the term multiplying r/α.
In line 3 the struck factor after ∂(1/r)/∂x is '· r/α · ∂x/∂t'-like (a substitution δx = −(r/α)ẋ), not just '· r/α'.
The last line likely reads '−4 (∂r/∂t)(∂r'/∂t)/(rr) − [struck]'; the second factor is uncertain.
